records.name: Personalised neoantigen (mRNA) vaccines
records.tldr: A vaccine designed for one person supplies instructions for selected sequences from that person's tumour. The design alone does not show that its targets are displayed, recognised or clinically useful.
records.summary:
Personalised neoantigen mRNA vaccines encode selected tumour-derived sequences to support antigen-directed immunity. Credible source sequence, delivery, peptide display, T-cell recognition and clinical benefit are separate questions.

Merck and Moderna reported in August 2026 that intismeran autogene (V940/mRNA-4157) with pembrolizumab met recurrence-free and distant-metastasis-free survival endpoints in INTerpath-001 in completely resected stage IIB-IV melanoma. This is the companies' interim report about a combination and population, rather than a finding about every cancer vaccine or a regulatory approval.

Rojas and colleagues' 2023 pancreatic phase 1 study treated 16 people with atezolizumab and autogene cevumeran, followed by chemotherapy in 15. The association between an immune response and recurrence-free survival does not isolate the vaccine's causal contribution. A phase 2 resected-pancreatic study, NCT05968326, is active but not recruiting in its registry record.

Other named V940 records have different stages: NCT06077760 in lung cancer is phase 3, NCT06307431 in renal cancer is phase 2, and NCT06305767 in bladder cancer is phase 1/2. The cutaneous squamous-cell study NCT06295809 is terminated for business reasons; that status is not an efficacy result. These are individual registry examples, not an exhaustive trial inventory.

notes: These vaccines aim to recruit or amplify T cells with receptors that can recognise the selected peptide together with HLA. Innate sensing and the specific adaptive response interact, but are different observations. Antigen in a supporting context can select matching cells to activate and increase in number; vaccination does not normally rewrite the receptor genes of each mature cell. A useful matching population may have been rare before treatment.

Priming is initial activation of a naive T cell, with dendritic-cell display and supporting signals contributing. A cell translating vaccine RNA can present antigen it makes, while cross-presentation places externally acquired antigen on class I HLA. Successful priming and later tumour attack remain separate. The responding cells must reach the tumour, find an appropriate displayed target and retain useful function. These are dependencies, not a guaranteed or strictly timed chain. A shared processing defect can limit several targets; adding source sequences does not automatically remove it. Useful killing and durable benefit need their own outcome measurements.

In a fictional study, peptide-reactive cells increase in sampled blood after vaccination. This supports a response in that compartment, not entry into the tumour, recognition of naturally processed antigen or prevention of recurrence. Repeating the blood measurement cannot settle the missing tumour-recognition or clinical comparison. Rare or unavailable matching cells, unsuitable delivery, poor display or supporting signals, and later access or functional barriers call for different measurements.

Consider invented, compatible blood reports. Before dosing, clone Q is not detected by an assay that cannot reliably detect it below 0.1% of sampled receptor units. After dosing, Q represents 1%. This is first detection in these samples and is consistent with enrichment. Non-detection did not prove absence from the blood, much less the whole body. There is no measured baseline for an exact observed fold change, and compatible absolute-cell counts are needed to infer expansion rather than only a frequency change.

A separate peptide-stimulation test of the fictional cell mixture responds, but does not link that response to Q. It therefore does not assign specificity to Q or demonstrate recognition of the natural tumour. Likewise, a tenfold rise in a sampled receptor sequence reports increased representation, rather than proving a newly created receptor, absolute cell expansion, tumour killing or benefit. The 0.1%, 1% and tenfold examples are invented teaching premises with comparable sampling and methods, not patient results or clinical thresholds.

Target number, formulation, combination and timing belong to the particular product. The V940 sponsor description specifies up to 34 encoded neoantigens; Rojas and colleagues used autogene cevumeran with up to 20 in their pancreatic study. Neither number is a universal selection score or manufacturing rule. Tolerability and added benefit require evidence for the actual regimen and population; a personalised sequence does not itself establish low toxicity.

TNBC-MERIT illustrates why immune-response denominators retain their assay. The 2026 report evaluated 14 participants after standard treatment for early triple-negative breast cancer. Overnight peptide-stimulated PBMC ELISpot detected responses in 12 of the 14. Eight had enough remaining cells for additional testing after 1.5 weeks of culture and stimulation of separated CD4 and CD8 cells. Every participant had a response by at least one ELISpot approach, which is a different observation from the direct-assay 12 of 14. Culture can change the number and state of responders and the specimen represented. These immune results in a noncomparative intravenous RNA-lipoplex study do not isolate recurrence-prevention benefit.

The protocol specifies dose, route, cadence, duration, combinations, safety monitoring and stopping rules. Batch release does not establish a safe dose or beneficial schedule. There is no general chemotherapy off-week, checkpoint-overlap or concurrent-targeted-drug rule for every cancer vaccine: mechanistic compatibility is a question for study in the actual regimen and population. Use controls, an informative baseline where appropriate, and a prespecified sampling plan. A comparison record names specimen compartment and time, preparation, stimulus or reagent, input-cell denominator, background controls and a prespecified response rule. A percentage within a CD8 gate, spots per million PBMCs and relative receptor frequency describe different quantities. Technical repeats from one sample are not reproducibility across people. Choosing a different test after seeing the result can favour a positive story, so retain the original response rule and any changed conditions. Safety requires systematic adverse-event collection rather than inference from an immune-response curve.
records.principle: A protocol selects tumour-derived sequences and encodes them in an RNA product. Delivery, presentation and priming then require testing. Target count, formulation, route and combinations are product-specific rather than universal features of the platform.

records.name: Neoantigen
records.tldr: A peptide arising from altered tumour sequence can be an immune target if it is displayed and recognised. Prediction alone does not show safe tumour killing.
records.summary:
A tumour sequence change can produce a new peptide sequence, but the altered sequence, its expression, HLA presentation and T-cell recognition are separate findings. Candidate sources include substitutions, frameshifts, fusions and altered RNA joins; a workflow that assessed one class has not necessarily assessed the others.

Computational ranking can consider binding, expression and clonality. In the TESLA study, Wells and colleagues combined tumour-normal exomes, tumour RNA and HLA typing, then tested selected peptides for HLA binding and recognition by existing patient-matched T cells. The study focused on small somatic variants and class I antigens; it did not validate every fusion or splice source, every new response a vaccine might induce, or clinical benefit from a vaccine. A candidate peptide and a favourable prediction do not establish safe recognition of naturally presenting tumour cells.

notes: Once the recognition mechanism is clear, a candidate source list precedes HLA matching, target selection and product construction. Confirm alteration identity, tumour specificity and biological support first. DNA, RNA and protein answer different questions, and a longer list can add uncertain calls as well as genuine candidates. A DNA alteration can nominate a possible sequence without establishing the processed peptide that a conventional T cell will recognise.

For tumour DNA, retain local usable coverage, artefacts, tumour fraction and copy number with the call. For matched normal DNA, absence is conditional on suitable sampling, coverage and detection limits. Tumour RNA can support an altered transcript, but comes from a mixture of cells and depends on expression depth and processing. Protein or peptide detection is a further observation with its own method coverage, cell-of-origin question and detection limits; none of these measurements can simply stand in for the others.

A cancer-cell fraction estimate describes the sampled cancer cells, whereas truncal describes ancestry shared across sampled branches; a subclonal alteration belongs to a subset. One small biopsy need not establish the distribution across every site. Read fraction and ancestry do not show that a peptide is displayed, and an unobserved region or insufficiently sampled alteration remains a gap rather than a demonstrated negative.

In an invented comparison, candidate A has a supported tumour DNA alteration, no support in adequately assessed normal DNA and observed mutant RNA. It has progressed further as a source candidate, but processing, HLA display and T-cell recognition remain untested. Candidate B has tumour DNA support but inadequate normal coverage, so tumour specificity is still unresolved. These are evidence questions, not a numerical ranking algorithm.

Two more fictional candidates illustrate bounded negatives. Candidate C has only a weakly supported RNA junction and needs reproducibility and artefact checks. Candidate D has strong DNA support but no RNA detection in a shallow assay, which cannot establish that the transcript is absent. None of A to D has demonstrated HLA presentation or T-cell recognition merely from these starting observations.

Prepared specimens and analysis can introduce misleading candidates through fixation damage, contamination, misalignment or uncertain junctions. The chosen reference transcript also matters when translating an altered sequence. Preserve specimen identity, coordinates and alleles, transcript/reference, method and software versions, usable coverage, thresholds and manual decisions so the result can be traced to its source. A filter or annotation is not independent proof of function.

Parkhurst and colleagues found neoantigen-reactive cultured lymphocyte populations in 62 of 75 people with gastrointestinal cancers. About 1.6% of the tested protein-changing mutant gene products were recognised, and 99% of the recognised determinants were unique to one person. This is a selected study and assay result, not the probability that any mutation is processed, displayed or useful in breast cancer. Applying 0.016 to 60 fictional candidate mutations gives 0.96, about one, as an arithmetic illustration only.

In a fictional comparison, the same expressed mutation produces a nine-amino-acid peptide that is displayed by person A's HLA-A*02:01 and meets a matching receptor. Person B's tested classical class-I variants bind no mutation-spanning peptide adequately; a possible class-II response is a different question. If A's tumour later loses the required HLA allele, the mutation can remain while that recognition route fails. Several candidates sharing that allele do not provide independent protection. Tumour-specific sequence also does not guarantee that its receptor avoids unrelated healthy-tissue targets.

records.name: Neoantigen candidate selection
records.tldr: Choosing vaccine targets means tracking what supports each candidate and which failures they share. More candidates or a better computer score do not by themselves show broader, safer tumour recognition.
records.summary:
A neoantigen design board links source alterations, encoded sequence windows, peptide and human leukocyte antigen (HLA) pairs, experimental evidence and unresolved dependencies. It compares a set of candidates for a stated purpose rather than turning one score into proof of a therapeutic target. A source event can generate several peptide windows, so candidate count and independent tumour coverage differ.

The evidence ladder has separate steps. Tumour-normal sequence comparison can support an alteration, and mutant RNA can support a sampled transcript without proving protein production or processing. A processing or binding prediction is a model result. Recovered HLA-associated peptide supports the sampled preparation without settling cell origin, receptor recognition or safety. A controlled T-cell response supports the tested stimulus; controlled recognition or killing of naturally presenting tumour cells tests a more direct function. Tissue distribution, persistence, safety and clinical benefit still need their own evidence. A suitable clinical comparison estimates benefit for that population, product and setting, without automatic transfer elsewhere.

One mutation can supply several windows or pairs, and several class-I alleles can share beta-2 microglobulin (B2M) and processing requirements. A fictional row M simply ends an otherwise unchanged protein early, whereas row N shifts the reading frame and creates an altered tail. N supplies a possible altered sequence; M's stop label alone does not. Neither establishes display or recognition. Reconstruct the actual transcript and sequence, and assess transcript-context-dependent decay rather than treating every truncating event alike.

A fictional board has ten rows, A to J, from nine events. A and B share Event 1 and allele X: A has supported alteration and mutant RNA, while B is another predicted window. C comes from Event 2, also through X, with an HLA-associated peptide identified but cell origin and recognition unresolved. J comes from Event 9 through X and has controlled tumour-cell recognition, leaving healthy-tissue specificity and durability open. These four rows share X despite their different evidence. Extra windows do not independently protect that shared display route.

The other fictional rows expose different gaps. D comes from Event 3 through allele Y and has a peptide-stimulated response without natural tumour-recognition evidence. E, Event 4 through Y, has a broad estimated cancer-cell fraction but weak RNA support. F, Event 5 through Z, has RNA and display-prediction agreement but may cover a small subclone. G, Event 6, uses class II and has a peptide-responsive helper population; which cells present it and in what context remain questions. H, Event 7 through Y, has a credible tumour-specific sequence but a similar healthy sequence needing specificity tests. I, Event 8 through Z, has a strong rank with limited model support for that allele. No universal clinical A-to-J order follows.

Re-read that board under two separate fictional reports, assuming X, Y and Z are classical class-I alleles. Loss of X directly challenges A, B, C and J, without establishing failure of Y or Z. A shared B2M-supported class-I display defect instead challenges A to F and H to J. G's class-II route requires separate presenting-cell and helper-response evidence; it is not an established rescue. Each row's original uncertainty remains. Ten windows from one alteration restricted to a lost allele increase the count without restoring that route.

If only one experiment can run, state which uncertainty it addresses and what either result would mean. Testing D against naturally presenting tumour cells, with appropriate controls, is one defensible choice. A positive connects the response to those tested cells under those conditions. A negative prompts checks of processing, display, cell state and assay adequacy. Neither result estimates patient benefit, and another experiment may be preferable for another stated goal.

Keep prediction tasks and units visible. Fictional K has a 0.4% eluted-ligand rank and L a predicted competitive-binding half-maximal inhibitory concentration (IC50) of 40 nanomolar (nM). The numerical values cannot rank K against L: one is a reference-relative score and the other an assay-concentration estimate. IC50 is not automatically an equilibrium binding constant. Compare matched outputs for the exact allele and model/version; a percentile is not a probability of benefit. Differential agretopicity compares mutant and normal predictions and inherits their uncertainty, rather than measuring escape from tolerance or natural recognition.

An estimated cancer-cell fraction is not a photograph of every cell or evidence that a mutation is truncal across all lesions. Purity, local copy number and altered-copy count affect interpretation of the raw variant read fraction. Similarly, a peptide list is a recovered subset with cell, HLA class, time, capture, database and confidence rules attached. Non-detection requires sensitivity context, and artificial peptide loading can bypass a tumour's own processing. State what was actually tested rather than moving a candidate to a later rung by inference.

A set can double-count correlated windows and correlated model assumptions. Model agreement is not independent validation; a weighted ensemble needs appropriate held-out evaluation for its task, alleles and population. Class-I and class-II choices can support different response components without guaranteeing recognition or overcoming a shared defect. Immunodominance can concentrate a measured response on a few offered targets. Epitope spreading means additional detected recognition beyond the encoded targets; it is not a substitute for a clinical comparison.

Maintain selection and exclusion reasons, the two sequences in a mutant-normal comparison, exact HLA protein names, specimen and assay context, model versions, manual overrides and the authorised construct version. Record the strongest observed support and the unresolved question beside each candidate. These are evidence-reading and traceability rules, not a validated scoring formula, a compulsory assay sequence or a personal treatment recommendation.

In a fictional evidence notebook, peptide A is identified in a mixed-tissue HLA preparation, an A-HLA multimer labels blood cells, post-dose cells produce more spots after A stimulation, and a receptor sequence becomes relatively more frequent. Record identification confidence and cell origin for the first result, allele and staining denominator for the second, and background, viability and culture-expansion history for the third. The sequence result neither identifies which cells made the spots nor proves an absolute increase in that receptor-bearing population. Natural recognition of tumour cells has not been tested and remains a visible gap. A controlled positive tumour-cell assay would strengthen that target under the tested conditions while leaving healthy-tissue safety and patient benefit separate.

Three physical workflows illustrate that separation. Immunopeptidomics can capture HLA-peptide complexes on an antibody-coated support, release connected peptide molecules and identify their sequences by mass spectrometry. A tetramer puts four specified peptide-HLA units on a shared laboratory scaffold to bind sampled T cells; this is not a native four-HLA receptor. In ELISpot, cells incubate over an antibody-coated capture membrane, then cells are removed and the membrane is washed before developed spots are read. Recovered peptides, reagent binding and secretion-associated spots do not by themselves measure tumour killing. Molecular shapes and illustrative spot counts are schematic rather than quantitative biological observations.

records.name: T-cell receptor
records.tldr: A conventional T-cell receptor recognises a peptide together with its HLA display. Recognition alone does not show killing.
records.summary:
A conventional alpha-beta T-cell receptor uses paired chains to recognise a peptide-HLA surface. Its recognition chains assemble with CD3 signalling partners, as demonstrated in the human TCR-CD3 structural study. CDR3 is an informative variable region, but neither a beta-chain sequence nor CDR3 alone specifies the complete paired receptor or its function.

Particular receptors can cross-react across peptide and HLA contexts; that does not establish a universal cross-reactivity rate. Paired receptor identity, binding, activation, target-cell death and clinical benefit require different evidence. A response by one reconstructed pair to peptide-loaded cells does not establish that another alpha-chain pairing recognises the same target, or that either kills naturally presenting tumour cells. Use irrelevant-target, HLA and target-only viability controls. Peptide loading can bypass natural processing, and contact diagrams are not healthy-tissue safety tests.

notes: A conventional alpha-beta TCR uses paired variable and constant domains to contact peptide plus HLA. The peptide sits in the HLA groove, not a separate TCR peptide pocket. CD3 signalling partners are distinct from recognition chains. Contact loops including junction-spanning CDR3 contribute, but other loops, the partner chain and HLA matter; beta-only or CDR3-only sequence is incomplete.

Cross-reactivity is recognition of multiple targets by a receptor. Defined receptor experiments demonstrated peptide/HLA cross-reactivity, not recognition of every allele by an arbitrary receptor or a universal rate. Greater affinity or a contact drawing does not establish healthy-tissue safety.

Sequencing reports sampled receptor identities and abundances under an operational clonotype definition. Paired alpha-beta identities are more complete than beta alone. Peptide-HLA multimer binding, stimulus-induced cellular response, target-cell death and clinical benefit are different endpoints. Include irrelevant-target, HLA and target-only viability controls; peptide-loaded cells can bypass natural processing.

Vaccination generally recruits or expands existing mature receptor specificities rather than rewriting each mature receptor. Engineered TCR therapy introduces selected receptor sequences. In either case, tested recognition must still connect to naturally presenting tumour targets, useful function and healthy-tissue safety. If one beta sequence pairs with different alpha chains, a positive reconstruction of one pair does not establish the other pair's function or tumour killing.

Source scope: teaching synthesis checked against the cited abstracts and specified accessible primary text on 9 November 2026; fictional examples are not clinical observations or treatment-selection rules.

Many measured conventional receptor-peptide-HLA interactions have micromolar dissociation constants; affinity, multiple contacts, CD4/CD8 coreceptors and the cellular signalling context contribute differently to activity. Stone and colleagues review those distinctions, rather than a universal affinity ranking against every antibody. One receptor type per cell is also a simplification: extra productive alpha chains and dual surface receptors have been documented. A chain sequence alone does not establish which assembled receptor provides the measured specificity.

records.name: HLA (human leukocyte antigen) and MHC
records.tldr: HLA molecules sit on cells and hold up small pieces of the cell's proteins for T cells to inspect. A T cell reads the fragment together with the particular HLA version holding it.
records.summary:
Human leukocyte antigen (HLA) is the human major histocompatibility complex (MHC) system, with two main classes of peptide-display molecule. Classical class I (HLA-A, HLA-B, HLA-C) has a heavy chain, beta-2 microglobulin (B2M) and a bound peptide, is found on most nucleated cells, usually displays peptides from proteins made inside the cell and is read by CD8 T cells. Class II (HLA-DR, HLA-DP, HLA-DQ) has alpha and beta chains with a bound peptide, is mainly on professional antigen-presenting cells (expression can be induced elsewhere), usually displays proteins processed in vesicles, often acquired from outside, and is read by CD4 T cells. These are common routes, not exclusive lists: cross-presentation puts externally acquired antigen on class I without making it class II, and a CD4 response is not proof of matching class I tumour display. CD4 and CD8 are coreceptors and usual recognition partners, not guarantees of cell function. Structural work shows the T-cell receptor lying across the peptide and HLA together (Garboczi et al., 1996), CD8 contacting the class I alpha2 and alpha3 domains and B2M (Gao et al., 1997) and CD4 engaging a separate class II region (Yin et al., 2012); these constructs do not define universal angles or functions.

HLA alleles are shared across people, and a person inherits a combination that is not necessarily unique. Each person inherits two copies each of HLA-A, HLA-B and HLA-C, so a cell can display up to six classical class I variants at once. The IPD-IMGT/HLA statistics page read on 9 November 2026 listed 46,146 HLA alleles, 31,311 class I and 14,835 class II (9,457 HLA-A, 11,328 HLA-B and 9,580 HLA-C alleles). Binding predictors estimate whether a peptide can fit a specified allele's groove, but processing, transport, loading and surface expression decide whether it is displayed. Sarkizova et al. (2020) profiled more than 185,000 peptides eluted from 95 mono-allelic cell lines to learn allele-specific motifs and build prediction models; that is allele-level data, not proof of any cell's display. Kaur et al. (2017) showed that HLA-C surface expression varies across individuals in an allele-specific manner, influenced by the structure of the peptide-binding cleft and peptide diversity; Apps and colleagues found lower HLA-C than HLA-A/B in the analysed healthy-donor peripheral blood lymphocytes with the A*02:01/B*44:02/C*05:01 haplotype; the magnitude differed between flow cytometry and mass spectrometry. This is a defined comparison, not a universal hierarchy. The small HLA-C peptide share observed by Schellens and colleagues in four B lymphoblastoid cell lines was also affected by their assignment method, which gave HLA-A/B precedence; it is not a universal biological fraction.

In cancer, class I HLA shows peptides to CD8 T cells and is also the main ligand for inhibitory receptors on natural killer cells, so losing it can hide a tumour from T cells while removing a brake on NK cells. HLA-E and HLA-G are nonclassical and vary little between people; HLA-E presents leader peptides from other class I molecules and binds the NK receptor CD94/NKG2A (Braud et al., 1998, with HLA-E tetramers). Tumours can lose a presenting allele (HLA loss of heterozygosity), alter processing or reduce expression, and allele-specific loss differs from complete loss of conventional class I display; targets on retained alleles may remain possible. Tran et al. (2016) documented a colorectal cancer lesion that progressed after T-cell therapy against mutant KRAS G12D, which had lost the chromosome 6 haplotype encoding the restricting HLA-C*08:02; this shows escape in one patient, not a rate. Typing, protein expression, recovered peptide, recognition and killing are different observations, and a conventional surface-target engager avoids peptide-HLA dependence while a peptide-HLA-directed engager keeps it.

B2M is the light chain of classical class I and does not span the membrane; class II contains no B2M, so CD4 T-cell recognition can remain when B2M is lost. B2M also partners other class I-like molecules: UniProt records heterotrimers with HLA-E, HLA-G, HLA-F and MR1 and lists CD1 interactions, and a B2M mutation caused deficiency of the neonatal Fc receptor FcRn in two siblings (Wani et al., 2006), so complete B2M loss can remove more than classical class I. Loss of one HLA allele can leave other presenting alleles usable, whereas loss of functional B2M impairs many class I targets at once, so several peptides on different alleles are not independent protection. A B2M variant, low RNA, absent surface class I and a blood B2M concentration are different observations: one variant does not show complete functional loss, and blood B2M does not count tumour peptide-HLA complexes. Zaretsky et al. (2016) linked a truncating B2M mutation to lost surface class I in one melanoma relapse after PD-1 blockade, which is a mechanism in that setting, not a frequency. Reduced class I display does not guarantee NK-cell killing, because activating signals are still needed.

CD4 help does not demonstrate the same target's class-I display. Some CD4 cells can themselves be cytotoxic: Cachot and colleagues directly tested tumour-specific human CD4 cells against tumour cells in defined assays. That result does not make every CD4 response cytotoxic or establish a treatment benefit.

records.name: mRNA and lipid nanoparticle manufacturing
records.tldr: Making an RNA cancer vaccine means copying a specified DNA template into a message, purifying it and preparing the chosen delivery formulation. Each lot needs its own quality checks before use.
records.summary:
An RNA vaccine starts with an approved sequence and product specification. Enzymes transcribe a DNA template outside living cells, and the RNA is purified, tested and prepared in the chosen delivery formulation. The cap, untranslated regions, coding sequence, poly(A) strategy and chemical building blocks are specified for that product. Nucleoside modification is not a universal requirement: the TNBC-MERIT and Rojas pancreatic studies used uridine RNA-lipoplex products. Cell-free transcription does not describe every upstream DNA-template manufacturing step, and neither all RNA products nor their downstream handling share one process.

Personalisation connects the source tumour information, intended RNA and protein, recipient and manufactured lot. The manufacturing clock needs its start and end as well as the product and setting. In TNBC-MERIT, manufacturing runs were conducted during 2019 and the reported sample-receipt-to-vaccine-release interval averaged 69 days, ranging from 34 to 125; optimising turnaround was not the study aim. Those observations do not set a duration for every personalised vaccine. Formulation, testing, review, queues and failed-lot handling belong to the actual production plan. Consistent manufacture, permission to administer and evidence that treatment benefits patients remain separate questions.

Two details matter when reading a product description. First, double-stranded RNA can arise from the transcription step itself: in one study T7 polymerase started transcription from a promoter-less DNA end and made an antisense strand that paired with the intended RNA and stimulated the innate sensor MDA5, and the effect fell with modified nucleotides or a lower magnesium concentration (Mu and colleagues). Purification was tested separately: HPLC removed contaminants including double-stranded RNA from nucleoside-modified transcripts and raised translation 10 to 1,000-fold in primary cells (Karikó and colleagues), and a cellulose method removed at least 90 per cent of double-stranded RNA with over 65 per cent recovery, taking out duplexes of 30 base pairs or longer while most of a 21 base-pair duplex remained (Baiersdörfer and colleagues). Second, a lipid nanoparticle is not the only formulation in use: in the pancreatic cancer phase I trial of autogene cevumeran each patient's vaccine held two uridine mRNA strands, each encoding up to 10 neoepitopes, formulated as lipoplex nanoparticles of about 400 nm made from the cationic lipid DOTMA and the phospholipid DOPE and given intravenously (Rojas and colleagues). Release testing is layered: a review of mRNA analytics lists identity and modification analysis, poly(A) tail, RNA content and integrity, double-stranded RNA and residual DNA as separate attributes, and a review of mRNA manufacturing cites a regulator-recommended residual DNA limit of 10 ng per dose (Losada and colleagues; Nowak and colleagues). Particle size and composition measurements do not by themselves show that usable RNA reaches the cytosol of the intended cell.

notes: A target list does not specify a finished message. Ribosomes translate RNA into protein, from which processing can generate fragments for HLA display. Keep the message, encoded protein and displayed fragments distinct. The manufacturing handoff retains the complete RNA sequence, each window and its source alteration, intended protein, cap, untranslated regions, initiation context, poly(A) strategy, chemical building blocks and delivery specification. It also retains the approved version, change rationale, prediction method and version, and the specimen, assay and conditions behind measured results. The intended altered residue must survive the handoff. A wrong sequence version, lost alteration or concealed biological edit cannot be repaired by a correct measurement on the wrong material. Follow the link from approved design through template, RNA, formulation, aseptic fill, released lot, transport and protocol administration; each handoff needs its own specification.

Consider a fictional message containing altered target windows A and B. A synonymous-codon revision is intended to preserve the full protein sequence, which must be checked before comparing RNA and protein behaviour. Shortening their spacer changes the combined protein and its junction, calling for renewed processing and display assessment. Substituting a modified uridine building block can retain the intended protein while changing sensing or translation, so purity and delivery need an appropriately matched comparison. An initiation-context revision is another distinct question: Kozak context spans the untranslated and coding boundary around the start codon. Kozak tested preproinsulin constructs, not a universal vaccine design. A trafficking signal directs the encoded protein towards a cellular compartment, and a helper segment can support CD4 responses in a particular design; neither is universally required. More reporter protein does not establish display of both targets, natural tumour recognition or prevention of recurrence. An expression model may lack the intended presentation pathway. A prediction names an uncertainty for a relevant assay rather than proving success or failure. Comparing a revision requires the exact old and new RNA and protein specifications and the reason for each edit.

The format changes what is made and what still needs to be tested. Solid-phase peptide synthesis assembles an amino-acid chain on a support, then releases and purifies it; antigen-presenting-cell loading or processing and priming remain biological questions. RNA supplies instructions, whether delivered in a specified nanoparticle or lipoplex. DNA and engineered vectors raise their own questions about expressing cells, duration and vector-specific risks. LNP and lipoplex labels can overlap in papers, so inspect composition and architecture. Record composition, RNA amount and integrity, particle properties and relevant biological activity for the chosen formulation. A new formulation or route can change behaviour even with the same message. Identity, purity, integrity, relevant activity, stability and handling are separate attributes: residual DNA, proteins, incomplete RNA and double-stranded RNA are not one measurement, and a low double-stranded-RNA signal does not establish sterility.

For a historical product comparison, TNBC-MERIT studied early-stage triple-negative breast cancer after standard therapy in a noncomparative phase I arm. Its intravenous, non-nucleoside-modified uridine RNA-lipoplex course had eight personalised administrations, six weekly followed by two every other week, ending at day 64. Two RNA strands each encoded up to ten selected windows. The first three evaluable participants also received a shared-antigen bridging vaccine while the personalised product was made. Rojas and colleagues studied a different intravenous uridine RNA-lipoplex product after pancreatic-cancer resection, within a sequence of atezolizumab, vaccine priming, chemotherapy and a later booster. These product and population records support their own feasibility and immune observations; neither single-arm sequence isolates a vaccine effect on recurrence.

KEYNOTE-942 instead randomised people with completely resected high-risk melanoma to V940 plus pembrolizumab or pembrolizumab alone. Its vaccine was given intramuscularly, up to nine administrations in three-week cycles. A separate 2025 primary protocol abstract, CT251 for the lung-cancer INTerpath-009 study, describes V940 as LNP-encapsulated; that abstract is formulation evidence, not the melanoma trial outcome report. The melanoma comparison tests adding that product to that backbone, not LPX against LNP. Neither acronym reveals the entire lipid recipe, RNA chemistry, cap, impurity limits or stability specification, and cross-trial percentages cannot rank formulations. These are historical study protocols rather than administration recommendations.

Quality review separates the antigen and construct, approved version and change control, manufactured lot, and clinical protocol and monitoring. GMP is a quality system, CMC an evidence package, a certificate of analysis a test-results document and batch release a disposition. A CDMO performs agreed activities without erasing applicable responsibilities. FDA's 2016 quality-agreement guidance addresses commercial manufacture and excludes investigational materials from its explicit scope, while describing the usefulness of such agreements before commercial use. The 1999 vaccine CMC document concerns licence applications; the 2011 therapeutic cancer-vaccine guidance concerns investigational clinical studies. These dated documents do not supply universal RNA release limits. Potency addresses relevant biological activity; expression can be one part of a mechanism, without proving presentation, tumour recognition or clinical benefit.

In a fictional spacer-revision comparison, A, B and C are three independently prepared matched material pairs, not people or doses. Each reported signal is a mean of two technical wells. Before and after, each preparation contains 1 mg RNA. Reporter signals are 100 to 104 for A, 98 to 101 for B and 102 to 100 for C; target-B display signals are 9 to 3, 8 to 3 and 10 to 4. All numbers are invented. The stipulated conditions keep formulation, cell model, method and observation time the same, with fixed viable-cell normalisation and a common reference within each assay. No-RNA and no-target-B controls are described as background and a reference gives its expected signal, but those are qualitative premises rather than supplied raw control data. The reporter is an expression surrogate, whereas the display assay reports relative cell-surface target-B peptide-HLA signal in one laboratory model.

Calculate each fictional change within its own assay. Reporter changes for A, B and C are +4, +3 and -2 units, or approximately +4.0%, +3.1% and -2.0%. Display decreases are 6, 5 and 6 units, or 66.7%, 62.5% and 60.0%, using the decrease divided by that pair's starting display signal. The two arbitrary-unit scales are not commensurate: reporter 100 cannot be compared with display 9, and nearby reporter values do not establish equivalent target display. Three preparations remain three independent units despite six technical wells. Equal RNA mass after a length change need not mean equal molecule counts, so length, integrity and appropriate input normalisation still matter.

The fictional table lacks raw wells and controls, assay precision and range, detection and quantification limits, comparison bounds and release limits. The qualitative control notes do not establish that either assay is fully validated. Investigate altered processing or display alongside assay and input effects before assigning a cause. A spacer revision changes the construct even when motivated by manufacture, so reusing earlier design or function evidence needs an explicit justification alongside any process review. Set and justify comparison criteria for the intended use; a process-only bridge cannot cover a changed message. Q5E's 2005 scope is cell-culture protein and polypeptide products: applying its comparison principles to this RNA example is an analogy, not an RNA regulatory determination. This panel cannot decide lot disposition, establish that the spacer caused the drop, prescribe further studies or convert an earlier laboratory result into natural tumour recognition or patient benefit.

Handling and release need the product's own evidence. A correct sequence can coexist with inadequate RNA integrity or functional activity. Shelf life and allowable storage excursions come from product-specific stability evidence. A report with acceptable identity and purity does not resolve an unassessed transport excursion. The quality function reviews relevant testing, stability and handling records before release, hold or rejection; a passing assay on a wrongly assigned vial cannot establish recipient identity or custody. A fictional LNP lot cannot borrow intravenous lipoplex handling instructions or infer sterility from nondetectable double-stranded RNA. After a facility change, unchanged final RNA mass alone does not bridge impurities, formulation, activity or stability. The one-formulation spacer example also cannot rank LPX against LNP or supply shelf life, handling instructions or clinical outcomes.

records.name: Batch release (lot disposition)
records.tldr: Batch release is the documented quality decision about one lot of a product. A set of passing test results supports that decision but is not the same thing, and a released lot has not been shown to help any patient.
records.summary: In the US, drug production and control records are reviewed and approved by the quality control unit before a batch is released or distributed, and any unexplained discrepancy or failure of a batch to meet a specification must be thoroughly investigated whether or not the batch has been distributed (21 CFR 211.192). The decision therefore draws on test results with their methods and acceptance criteria, manufacturing and deviation records, and the identity of the lot and product version; a certificate of analysis can summarise results but does not replace that review. FDA's 2022 guidance on out-of-specification results says the practice of repeating a test until a passing result is obtained and then disregarding the failing results without scientific justification is 'testing into compliance', which it calls unscientific and objectionable under CGMP. That guidance covers chemistry-based laboratory testing; it says it is not intended to address biological assays, so a copied retest procedure cannot be assumed to fit a cell or potency assay. A lot can be released, held pending review or rejected; a result that has not arrived is neither a pass nor a failure. Release of a lot is a quality decision, separate from regulatory authorisation of the product, from a patient's eligibility, and from evidence of clinical benefit.

A lot is identified material made under a defined manufacturing record, and a specification connects named tests and methods to acceptance criteria; ICH Q6B defines a specification as a list of tests, references to analytical procedures and acceptance criteria. Release concerns that lot, not the general reputation of its manufacturer.

What a release review brings together: test results with their methods and criteria, manufacturing and deviation records, lot and version identity, and stability and handling information. In US finished-drug rules the quality control unit reviews and approves production and control records before a batch is released or distributed (21 CFR 211.192). A certificate of analysis may summarise results but does not replace that review.

Dispositions. FDA's quality-systems guidance describes the quality unit approving or rejecting materials and drug products; US regulations give the quality unit authority to approve or reject materials and drug products (21 CFR 211.22(a)); other provisions describe quarantine or withholding from use while materials or products await release (211.80(d), 211.84(a), 211.142(a)). Hold pending review is a plain-language description of that unresolved disposition. A result that has not arrived is neither a pass nor a failure. Inference lesson: a spreadsheet that reports all tests passed because it lists only completed tests has lost the missingness information; with a required activity result pending, completed release is not established.

Out-of-specification handling. FDA's May 2022 guidance calls repeated testing until a pass followed by disregarding the failures without scientific justification testing into compliance, which it describes as unscientific and objectionable under CGMP. It asks that the number of retests be set in advance in a procedure and not adjusted according to results, and it contrasts averages: initial 89 then 90 and 91 per cent averages 90 and tends to confirm the failure, while 80 then 85 and 105 also averages 90 but presents a very different picture. Releasing despite an initial failure that has not been invalidated should follow a full investigation. The guidance applies to chemistry-based laboratory testing of drugs regulated by CDER and says it is not intended to address biological assays, so it cannot simply be copied for a cell or potency assay.

Release is a quality decision. It is separate from regulatory authorisation of the product, a patient's eligibility and evidence of benefit, and a released stamp on a report does not answer those. For US licensed biological products, manufacturer release follows completion of applicable tests under 21 CFR 610.1. Separately, under 610.2 FDA may require samples and protocols and, on notification, bar distribution until the relevant CBER or CDER Director releases the lot. These are distinct manufacturer and official-release steps; this example does not establish other jurisdictions' rules.

records.name: Cancer vaccines and oncolytic viruses
records.tldr: Cancer vaccines aim to support immune recognition of cancer targets. Oncolytic viruses can injure susceptible cancer cells; useful tumour-directed immunity and clinical benefit need separate evidence.
records.summary:
Cancer-vaccine strategies differ in purpose, target selection and supplied material. Infection-prevention vaccines reduce the risk from cancer-causing infections. Therapeutic strategies aim at cancer-associated targets, including after removal of visible disease. Personalised selection, shared targets and RNA or peptide delivery are separate design choices.

Oncolytic viruses are a related approach in which viral activity can injure susceptible tumour cells and release material that may support an immune response. Infection, tumour recognition and useful clinical control remain distinct. A product-specific result cannot establish benefit for every vaccine, virus, cancer or setting.

notes: Cancer-vaccine strategies seek useful recognition of cancer-associated targets. Their purpose is different from vaccination against an infection that can cause cancer: HPV and hepatitis B vaccines reduce infection-related cancer risk, rather than treat an established tumour. A therapeutic vaccine can be studied after removal of visible cancer to reduce recurrence risk; that timing does not turn it into infection prevention. Teaching recognition is an aim, not a guarantee that responding cells will reach and control the cancer.

Describe a vaccine along three independent axes: its purpose, how its targets are selected, and what material is supplied. Personalised selection uses information or material from one person's tumour and can still include targets shared with other people. Shared targets can be tumour-associated proteins or recurring mutation-derived neoantigens. Neither label proves that every cancer cell contains and displays the target. RNA can encode shared targets, and a personalised product can contain peptides. A three-axis comparison therefore classifies designs without ranking their effectiveness.

A designed product supplies planned antigen material or instructions for making it. An in-situ approach instead uses tumour material already within the body while trying to support presentation and immune activation. Injury or injection alone does not show that vaccination succeeded. These categories describe antigen sources; they do not determine route, peptide display, personalisation or clinical benefit. The dedicated in-situ vaccination and intratumoral immunotherapy records distinguish a learning strategy from a delivery route.

Brody's 2010 phase I/II study treated 15 people with low-grade B-cell lymphoma using low-dose radiation to one tumour and an injected CpG TLR9 agonist at that site. At distant untreated sites, one participant had a complete response and three had partial responses. This is evidence for a particular multicomponent regimen in that lymphoma group. It does not establish that every local injury creates a vaccine, that the same result occurs in breast cancer, or that this strategy outperforms a supplied-antigen vaccine.

Ott's 2017 melanoma study illustrates personalised selection without RNA delivery. Six people received a vaccine containing long peptides selected from their own tumours with poly-ICLC, an immune stimulus. The study demonstrated manufacturing feasibility and assay-defined antigen-reactive responses. Some T-cell preparations also recognised the person's tumour cells, while others did not under the tested conditions. This early, nonrandomised study cannot rank all peptide and RNA platforms or isolate the contribution of each ingredient.

Follow a proposed vaccine response through separate questions. Is the antigen supplied or available with suitable supporting signals? Is it processed and displayed, and are suitable cells primed or expanded? Do those cells reach the tumour, recognise naturally displayed targets and maintain useful function? Finally, does the complete intervention improve a clinical outcome with acceptable harms? Variation between tumour cells, differences in target display and immune restraint can affect different steps. The sequence is a way to investigate dependencies, not a promise that each stage follows automatically.

Manufacturing feasibility, immunogenicity and clinical benefit are different endpoints. An immune assay needs its stated cell population, supplied antigen, controls, sampling time and response definition. Reactivity in blood to added peptide does not by itself establish recognition of naturally processed targets on cancer cells; recognition in a model does not establish fewer recurrences. A clinical comparison needs the population, accompanying treatments, endpoint, follow-up and harms. A positive result at one level cannot substitute for the next.

Adding target sequences does not guarantee equally broad functional immunity. Responses can be concentrated on a subset of epitopes, a pattern called immunodominance; Ott's study found different response frequencies across selected targets and T-cell populations. A vaccine adjuvant is an ingredient intended to support an immune response. Adjuvant cancer treatment instead means treatment after the main treatment. These uses of the same word describe different things.

In a fictional study, an RNA product encoding shared tumour-associated antigens is given after surgery, and an antigen-reactive blood response is detected. Its purpose is therapeutic risk reduction, its target selection is shared, and its supplied material is RNA. Nothing in those facts demonstrates personalised manufacture, natural tumour recognition or reduced recurrence. Those conclusions require their own product, assay and clinical evidence.

records.name: Vaccine adjuvants
records.tldr: A vaccine adjuvant is an ingredient intended to support an immune response. Its effects depend on the antigen, formulation and exposure; more inflammation does not establish cancer benefit.
records.summary:
Vaccine adjuvants support the immune context in which antigen is encountered. Their actions can involve different sensing, recruitment, antigen-availability and activation pathways. Antigen specificity, delivery, useful priming and tumour control remain distinct questions.

The ingredient meaning differs from adjuvant cancer treatment after the main treatment. An adjuvant’s contribution needs a suitable comparison, and immune assay responses, clinical outcomes and harms need separate measurement.

Ingredients can affect recruitment, antigen availability, activation and supporting signals through different pathways. Mata-Haro's 2007 experiments studied monophosphoryl lipid A, an LPS-derived TLR4 agonist. In mice, its lower inflammatory toxicity relative to LPS was associated with biased TRIF signalling while retaining adjuvant activity. This is a defined molecule, comparison and model. It does not establish a universal safe amount, route-independent safety or a rule that more innate stimulation improves human cancer outcomes.

Delivery and adjuvant activity can overlap but answer different questions. Material entering a cell does not establish useful priming, and a lipid carrier's immune effects depend on its composition, payload, route and exposure. Recognition of antigen, entry into tumour tissue, useful function and safety remain separate requirements. Experience with an ingredient in an infection-prevention vaccine does not by itself establish efficacy in cancer treatment.

Ott's personal melanoma vaccine combined selected long peptides with poly-ICLC, a stabilised synthetic double-stranded RNA immune stimulus. The study's antigen-reactive responses concern that package. There was no randomised estimate of the adjuvant's independent contribution, so the result cannot determine what the same peptides would have done without it or rank every alternative adjuvant.

Hailemichael's 2013 mouse melanoma experiments found that a persistent short-gp100-peptide depot in incomplete Freund's adjuvant could draw vaccine-reactive T cells to the vaccination site, with dysfunction and deletion. A nonpersisting formulation shifted localisation toward tumours under the tested conditions. The study also found less sequestration and different activity with a longer peptide in the depot formulation. Persistence is therefore not automatically better, but these experiments do not show that every depot adjuvant fails in humans.

Assess presenting-cell activation, antigen-specific antibody or T-cell responses, persistence and harms with the cell population, units, background controls and sampling time stated. To isolate an adjuvant's contribution, use suitable comparisons with the same antigen and relevant conditions. Changing antigen, carrier and adjuvant together measures a package; it cannot assign the result to one ingredient. Clinical tumour outcomes require separate evidence from an immune assay.

A vaccine adjuvant is an immune-supporting ingredient, while adjuvant cancer treatment is given after the main treatment. Redness, fever or a high cytokine signal is not proof of useful antigen-specific immunity. A larger measured response may involve different cells, durability and harms, so neither more inflammation nor more stimulation is an automatic success criterion.

In a fictional comparison, formulations A and B contain the same antigen. A causes more redness; B gives a larger controlled antigen-specific assay response. A has a stronger observed local reaction and B a stronger response under the assay's definition, but neither result establishes cancer control. Check route, sampling, controls, persistence and harms, then the appropriate clinical outcomes, before assigning a benefit to an ingredient.

records.name: Immune surveillance and cancer immunoediting
records.tldr: Immune responses can control cancer and select which populations persist. Immunoediting is a testable framework, not a way to assign a phase or recurrence risk from one scan.
records.summary:
The claim. Immune surveillance concerns recognition and control of transformed cells. Immunoediting adds selection of the populations that persist. Elimination, equilibrium and escape are conceptual processes that can coexist or occur independently. Their assignment requires evidence of control, restraint or outgrowth and its mechanism; they are not a compulsory calendar for every clinical cancer. The immune system therefore both protects against cancer and shapes the cancers that emerge.

Who and when. Ehrlich 1909; Burnet 1957 and 1970 and Thomas 1959 stated the surveillance hypothesis. Stutman's 1974 finding that athymic nude mice were no more prone to chemically induced tumours seemed to refute it. Shankaran, Old and Schreiber showed in 2001 that mice lacking lymphocytes or interferon-gamma signalling develop more tumours and that tumours from immunodeficient mice are more immunogenic, which is the signature of editing. Dunn and colleagues named immunoediting in 2002; Schreiber, Old and Smyth reviewed it in 2011. Allison's 1996 CTLA-4 blockade and Honjo's PD-1 discovery gave it its therapy; Chen and Mellman's cancer-immunity cycle (2013) is its clinical map.

Evidence for. Immunodeficient mice develop more spontaneous and induced tumours. Organ transplant recipients on immunosuppression have higher rates of many cancers, not only virus-driven ones. Immune-cell and outcome associations vary across cancers and measurements. Some tumour studies show neoantigen depletion or HLA loss consistent with editing, with other explanations and sampling limits still relevant. Checkpoint inhibitors produce durable remissions in melanoma, lung, kidney, bladder and mismatch repair-deficient cancers, while mutation count, candidate neoantigens or viral origin alone do not establish an individual response.

Evidence against and limits. Nude mice retain immune functions and are not a clean comparison of every immune mechanism; Shankaran also noted that they do not completely lack functional T cells. The episode illustrates the importance of the precise model. Most cancers arise in people with normal immunity, and the immune system also promotes cancer through inflammation. Equilibrium is difficult to observe directly in humans. Immunotherapy fails in most patients with pancreatic, prostate and brain cancers, and the reasons are only partly understood.

Predictions that held or failed. Held: releasing checkpoints unleashes anti-tumour immunity; particular studies find loss of recognised antigens under immune pressure; adoptive transfer of tumour-reactive T cells can cure. Failed: most therapeutic cancer vaccines of the 1990s and 2000s; the expectation that boosting immunity non-specifically (interferon, interleukin-2 in most settings) would be broadly effective.

Therapies that came from it. Checkpoint inhibitors (ipilimumab, nivolumab, pembrolizumab and successors), CAR-T cells, tumour-infiltrating lymphocyte therapy (lifileucel), T-cell engagers, neoantigen mRNA vaccines and the use of mutational burden and mismatch repair deficiency as predictive biomarkers. It applies clonal evolution to the immune system as predator, draws on the microenvironment view for the mechanisms of escape, and entered the hallmarks in 2011.

Status: model experiments and human observations support immune control and selection. They do not establish a universal sequence of phases, the fraction of all cancers prevented, or a personal recurrence forecast.

notes: Immune surveillance concerns immune control of transformed cells. Immunoediting adds that immune pressure can alter which cancer populations persist. Elimination, equilibrium and escape describe processes that can coexist or occur independently, not a mandatory three-stage calendar. Shankaran’s genetically defined mouse experiments support lymphocyte and interferon-gamma contributions to control and selection. They do not measure what fraction of all human cancers immunity prevents.

Koebel used immune perturbation in chemical-carcinogenesis mouse models to demonstrate equilibrium; a quiet scan alone is not such an experiment. Matsushita combined sequencing, antigen recognition and immune comparisons in mouse sarcoma to support selection of pre-existing antigen-distinct clones. This is different from T cells creating every mutation that appears later.

Luksza followed 70 pancreatic ductal adenocarcinomas from 15 people longitudinally over ten years, comparing primary and recurrent tumours and modelling neoantigen quality and clonal fitness. Long-term survivors had stronger primary T-cell activity and recurrent tumours with fewer high-quality neoantigens under the model. This is human cohort and modelling evidence, not a vaccine experiment or direct observation of every selection event. Treatment and sampling history and model assumptions remain relevant.

In a fictional immune-pressure comparison, both arms begin with A/B counts of 80/20. Later, the control has 160/40 and the pressure arm 10/40. B is 20% versus 80% of the later populations, although its later count is 40 in both. Recognition and comparable conditions are separate evidence; a larger share does not mean that pressure created more B cells. This example is distinct from 900/100 becoming 90/90, where B’s share rises while its count falls.

An editing claim combines longitudinal populations or antigens, recognition or functional assays and relevant comparisons. Apparent antigen loss can instead reflect sampling, detection limits, expression change or another treatment. Neither sequencing alone nor a killing experiment reconstructs the whole history. One immune-rich sample, negative blood test or model cannot assign an individual postoperative phase, explain every recurrence or forecast personal risk; different lesions can face different pressures.

Immune escape can involve loss of a targeted antigen, altered HLA alleles or processing, defective inducible signalling, inhibition after entry or impaired access. Anagnostou found loss of putative neoantigens in checkpoint-resistant lung tumours with accompanying T-cell evidence. McGranahan described allele-specific HLA loss in lung cancer evolution. Montesion’s commercial pan-cancer genomic series contained 83,644 samples with HLA-I loss of heterozygosity in 17%; this assay-defined pan-cancer observation is not a breast-specific prevalence. Allele loss differs from reversible expression change or a B2M defect affecting class-I surface display.

In Zaretsky’s selected four-person melanoma relapse series, two cases had JAK1 or JAK2 loss-of-function changes with loss of the normal allele and another had a truncating B2M change. The JAK2-deficient relapse cells failed to increase interferon-gamma signalling, PD-L1 and class I while retaining interferon-alfa/beta responsiveness. Engineered JAK1- or JAK2-deficient melanoma cells were still recognized by the tested NY-ESO-1-specific T cells. Baseline display, inducibility, recognition and killing are separate dependencies; neither a JAK variant nor detectable HLA alone answers all of them.

In a fictional controlled comparison, both cultures have baseline class I; only the control increases its signal and surface display after interferon gamma. The candidate retains an interferon-alfa response, and restoring JAK2 restores the tested gamma response. With matched handling, viability and restoration controls, this supports a model-specific JAK2-dependent inducibility defect. It is not proof of a particular displayed peptide, safe clinical rescue, tumour access or useful killing. JAK1 and JAK2 have different interferon dependencies.

Treatment can select a pre-existing population and new changes can arise. Earlier specimens, retained alleles, expression, stimulation and controlled functional comparisons help test an escape explanation. Different sites may have different bottlenecks; several mechanisms may coexist. Blood tumour DNA alone does not identify a particular escape route. A proposed HLA-independent recognizer or combination still needs its own target, access, function and safety evidence, and a restored laboratory endpoint does not establish clinical benefit.

records.name: Solid-phase peptide synthesis
records.tldr: Peptides are built by holding the growing chain on a solid support and adding one amino acid at a time. Making the chain is a separate step from purifying it, confirming it is the right molecule and releasing it as a medicine.
records.summary: In solid-phase peptide synthesis the growing chain is held on a resin while protected amino acids are added one at a time and soluble reagents are washed away; the finished chain is then cleaved from the resin. Sequence changes how hard this is: peptides rich in aggregation-prone sequences are difficult, and a 2014 report described automated backbone protection that improved handling, quality and yield of several challenging sequences. For personalised cancer vaccines, an automated flow synthesiser made 30-mer peptides in under 35 minutes and 15 to 16-mers in under 20 minutes, with purity comparable to or higher than other methods (Truex et al., 2020). The same paper reports what the earlier route cost: of 598 immunising peptides designed and ordered in earlier studies, 400 (67 per cent) could be synthesised and purified to at least 95 per cent purity, with an average lead time of 18 to 20 weeks for 20 peptides, and a commercial vendor returned 10 of 29 test peptides at more than 95 per cent HPLC purity; these 29 peptides had been deliberately selected because they were particularly difficult and time-consuming to make, rather than as a typical vendor workload. In that paper mass spectrometry of the unpurified peptides showed the desired mass as the main product for all 29, and purity was measured separately by analytical reverse-phase HPLC. Synthesis, purification, identity testing and lot release are separate steps, and a peptide that is made and pure has not been shown to prime T cells or to benefit a patient.

notes: The cycle, as run in the neoantigen paper. Truex et al. (2020) used Fmoc-based solid-phase synthesis: the C-terminal amino acid was loaded onto a resin, the terminal protecting group was removed (Fmoc removal was followed by UV detection), the next activated protected amino acid was coupled in excess and soluble reagents were washed away, and the cycle repeated. Flow conditions achieved amide-bond coupling in seconds where standard batch methods need minutes to hours. The finished chain was cleaved and lyophilised as a trifluoroacetic acid salt.

Sequence difficulty. Chain association (aggregation) of growing peptides blocks coupling, and double coupling does not help because the cause is intermolecular association; introducing removable backbone protection improved handling, quality and yield of several challenging sequences (Abdel-Aal et al., 2014). Washing removes soluble material but does not repair a faulty chain. This study did not make every peptide equally easy.

After cleavage the crude peptide is a mixture needing purification and characterisation, and the synthesiser's last step is not a release decision. In Truex et al. electrospray mass spectrometry of the unpurified products showed the desired mass as the main product for all 29 test peptides, while purity was measured separately by analytical reverse-phase HPLC at 214 nm, with greater than 95 per cent HPLC purity used as the purity criterion. In that deliberately difficult 29-peptide commercial-vendor comparison, 17 peptides were synthesised, 10 passed after purification, and 7 stayed at 89 to 94 per cent even after two or three rounds. The 95 per cent figure is that paper's criterion, not a clinical-release threshold.

Assay peptides versus the clinical product. The same paper made 15 to 16-mer peptides for immune-assessment assays and longer immunising peptides of up to 30 residues for vaccination, and its authors describe clinical-grade manufacture as something they envision. Making an assay peptide does not show manufacture of a formulated, released vaccine product, and chemical assembly does not select a useful cancer antigen or show benefit. A shorter instrument run does not establish the turnaround of the whole program.

records.name: CDMO (contract development and manufacturing organisation)
records.tldr: A contract organisation carries out agreed work developing or making medicines for a client. Its service label does not show which tasks, quality evidence or responsibilities an agreement covers.
records.summary:
A contract development and manufacturing organisation performs agreed development or manufacturing work for a client. Its scope may include process development, synthesis, formulation, filling or analytical testing; a service label alone does not say which activities an agreement covers.

The US FDA's November 2016 quality-agreement guidance addresses commercial drug manufacture and recommends documenting each party's activities. The owner's quality unit approves or rejects contracted products or services, and the contract facility retains its own applicable current good manufacturing practice responsibilities. An agreement cannot delegate statutory responsibilities. Investigational material is outside the guidance's explicit scope, although FDA describes quality agreements as useful in research and development. Contractor experience, a contract or a passing identity result does not by itself establish release, authorisation or clinical benefit for a product.

notes: Scope must be read from the contract. A partner may develop a process, synthesise a molecule, formulate it, fill vials or run analytical testing, and a service label does not show which of these a contract covers. FDA's November 2016 quality-agreement guidance treats owner and contract facility as both responsible for CGMP and says contract analytical laboratories are covered.

The agreement assigns activities but cannot contract away responsibilities. FDA states that quality agreements cannot be used to delegate statutory or regulatory CGMP responsibilities. The guidance is written for commercial manufacture and does not explicitly cover investigational material, though FDA believes quality agreements can be valuable in research and development arrangements. ICH Q10 section 2.7 extends the quality system to outsourced activities, with the pharmaceutical company ultimately responsible.

Handoff inference. A controlled handoff connects the approved design version to materials, records and the resulting lot. If a contractor proposes an edit and supplies a passing identity result on the revised lot, the missing items are the authorised version and approval of the edit, assessment of affected product properties and the full quality package. Identity alone does not show activity, authorisation or benefit, and sharing a contractor does not establish comparability.

A contractor's experience or a facility's track record does not establish release of a particular lot, and manufacturing acceptance, clinical-program authorisation and efficacy are separate questions.

records.name: Platform and personalised components of a product
records.tldr: Some parts of a personalised treatment are reused for every recipient, such as the manufacturing process. Others are chosen for one person, such as the sequence of the vaccine or the person's own cells. Each actual batch still needs to be checked on its own.
records.summary: Individualised products reuse some components and personalise others, and the two need separate evidence. In the phase 1 study of autogene cevumeran in resected pancreatic cancer (Rojas et al., 2023), individual vaccines of up to 20 neoantigens per patient were made in real time as uridine mRNA-lipoplex nanoparticles; 16 patients received atezolizumab and the vaccine, 15 subsequently received mFOLFIRINOX chemotherapy, and new neoantigen-specific T cells were detected in 8 of the 16 patients, and it shows one defined design carrying individual messages, not that all RNA vaccines share a recipe or outcome. In mice, a peptide-TLR-7/8a conjugate platform was built to self-assemble into nanoparticles of uniform size (about 20 nm) whatever the peptide, to address the physicochemical variability of neoantigens (Lynn et al., 2020). For autologous CAR T cells, FDA's 2024 guidance notes variability in the starting cells and recommends maintaining chain of identity from collection to administration, with at least two unique identifiers on labels of autologous products. A shared process and specification can support consistent handling and repeatable testing, but they do not establish that a new sequence or a changed process is equivalent to an earlier one, that a lot made for one recipient can be accepted on another recipient's results, or that the encoded targets are presented and recognised in a patient. 'Platform' here is a descriptive term for reuse, not a regulatory designation.

notes: The single question to ask: is this feature deliberately reused across recipients, or selected for this recipient? Personalisation may concern an antigen sequence, a receptor sequence, the person's own cells or a combination, and need not mean that every reagent or step is redesigned. The answer depends on the program.

Platform is a teaching description of reuse and not a regulatory designation or authorisation. Reuse can support consistent handling, shared process learning and repeatable testing, and the two sides commonly work together; neither wins on efficacy by itself.

Shared process evidence informs but does not replace lot-level evidence. Inference lesson: if recipients A and B share RNA features and formulation but carry different antigen messages, a lot made for A that passes identity and quality checks does not allow lot B to be accepted; B must match its own specification and meet its own applicable checks, with traceability.

Different kinds of personalisation. Rojas et al. (2023) made individual mRNA-lipoplex vaccines of up to 20 neoantigens in real time (phase 1: 16 received atezolizumab and vaccine, followed by mFOLFIRINOX in 15). Lynn et al. (2020) built peptide conjugates to self-assemble into nanoparticles of about 20 nm whatever the peptide, to address neoantigen variability in mice. FDA's 2024 CAR T guidance notes variability in starting cells and recommends maintaining chain of identity from collection to administration, with at least two unique identifiers on autologous product labels. An individually selected receptor and an individual's own cells are different personalisation.

Quality categories. FDA's 1999 vaccine CMC guidance asks for characterisation with respect to identity, purity, potency and stability; it is dated and scoped to vaccine applications, so it illustrates categories and is not a rulebook for every individualised modality. No universal personalised-product cutoff exists. Passing release criteria does not show that antigens were selected correctly, presented naturally or that treatment benefits people.

The FDA also uses Platform Technology Designation for a separate formal programme under section 506K. Its May 2024 draft guidance describes designation requests and eligibility factors. Shared components or a manufacturing recipe do not by themselves establish that designation; platform in this entry means the described reuse of product components.

records.name: Randomised trial
records.tldr: A study that assigns eligible participants to interventions by chance. This reduces treatment-selection bias but does not guarantee identical groups, flawless follow-up or benefit.
records.summary: A randomized trial assigns eligible consenting participants to interventions by chance. Concealing the next assignment protects enrolment against foreknowledge; blinding concerns awareness after assignment. These are different design features. Randomization reduces treatment-selection confounding but leaves possible chance imbalance, missing outcomes and limits on applicability. The comparator, endpoint, analysis and conduct determine what the comparison establishes.

notes: Concealed chance assignment is different from predictable alternation between A and B. Allocation concealment hides the next assignment during enrolment; blinding concerns who knows the assigned treatment afterwards and may not be feasible for every intervention. Report sequence generation, allocation, who was blinded, assigned-group analyses, exclusions, dropout, missing assessments, treatment changes and unequal follow-up. Chance can balance measured and unmeasured factors on average without guaranteeing identical groups in one trial. Random assignment is not random sampling from a population: consenting eligible volunteers remain selected.

Controls can be standard care, standard care plus placebo or another protocol-defined option, not automatically no treatment. A fictional single-group Drug A study showing shrinkage supports an activity question for further study; it does not isolate added survival benefit from selection, natural history and other care. A randomized A-plus-usual-care versus usual-care comparison can test the added effect under sound conduct and analysis, while a volunteer cannot choose their randomized assignment or be promised benefit. A chance-assigned two-group phase 2 trial is randomized even though it is not phase 3.

records.name: RNA
records.tldr: RNA is a family of molecules with several jobs. Messenger RNA provides a protein-making template; other RNAs help build, regulate or carry out cellular processes.
records.summary: RNA, short for ribonucleic acid, uses ribose and usually uracil in place of DNA’s thymine. It is often single-stranded but can fold through internal pairing. Messenger RNA carries a coding template; ribosomal RNA contributes to ribosome structure and catalysis; transfer RNA brings amino acids; regulatory RNAs influence other molecules. Many nuclear messages receive a 5-prime cap and poly(A) tail and have introns removed by splicing before translation, but these features are not universal to all RNAs. Ribosomes read a coding sequence in codons to produce a polypeptide; processing, folding and localization follow.

notes: RNA abundance reflects production, processing and degradation. Short sequencing reads do not prove that a full-length intact message was captured. A noncoding RNA can function without becoming a protein, and reverse transcription copies RNA into DNA in relevant biological contexts. RNA amount does not determine a fixed protein amount or activity.

After successful delivery, a supplied ordinary mRNA can be translated at cytoplasmic ribosomes; that translation step does not require the message to enter the nucleus. Supplying a message, measuring endogenous tumor RNA and demonstrating nuclear DNA modification are separate observations. The NHGRI vaccine example illustrates supplied RNA instructions, not a general cancer-efficacy claim.
